claims.claim: The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines conformity as the adjustment of one's opinions, judgments, or actions so that they become more consistent with the opinions, judgments, or actions of other people or with the normative standards of a social group or situation.
Conformity includes temporary outward acquiescence (compliance) as well as more enduring private acceptance.
People conform for two primary reasons: concern about what others think of them (normative influence) and reliance on other people as a source of information (informational influence).

Normative social influence is conformity aimed at fitting in, feeling good, and being accepted; informational social influence is conformity based on the belief that the group has correct information, especially when the situation is ambiguous; the distinction is attributed to Deutsch and Gerard (1955).
In Solomon Asch's line-judgment studies of the 1950s, confederates gave obviously wrong answers on some trials and about 76% of participants conformed at least once by giving the wrong answer too.

Conformity rates vary: replications show they depend on the participant's age, gender, and sociocultural background, and some research suggests overall conformity rates are lower now than in Asch's era.

Conformity increases with the size of the majority up to a point (roughly five to seven people) and then levels off; the presence of one dissenter drops conformity rates to near zero; conformity is more likely when responses are public than when they are private.

The conformity effect appears in virtually every culture studied, but conformity is higher in collectivist countries such as Japan and China than in individualistic countries such as the United States (Bond & Smith, 1996).

Descriptive norms — what most people actually do — guide behavior when people are uncertain, and misperceived norms can steer behavior toward harm, such as students who overestimate peers' drinking and drink more to match an imagined norm (Cialdini, Reno, & Kallgren, 1990; Neighbors et al., 2007).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reported conformity proportions and the group-size ceiling vary across sources and replications.
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e reports 76% of participants conforming at least once (Asch, 1955) and conformity increasing with majority size up to seven people before leveling off and decreasing slightly.
Noba (Burger) reports the same 76% figure (Asch, 1956) but describes conformity increasing with more confederates up to about five.
Replication research (Bond & Smith, 1996; Bond, 2005) finds conformity rates depend heavily on procedure, sample, age, and culture.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the 76% figure to Asch with both the 1955 and 1956 citations available, and states the group-size claim as 'up to roughly five to seven people, then levels off' to cover both sources' ranges. The honest note that rates vary across replications and populations is included, sourced to OpenStax and Noba.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The APA Dictionary's conformity entry does not itself define normative versus informational influence.
positions: APA Dictionary of Psychology defines conformity and notes the compliance/private-acceptance range, but not the two-influence distinction.
OpenStax Psychology 2e and the Noba module both present normative and informational influence, citing Deutsch and Gerard (1955).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the APA entry only for the working definition and the compliance/acceptance nuance, and attributes the normative/informational distinction to Deutsch and Gerard (1955) as relayed by OpenStax and Noba. No source is cited for a claim it does not support.

sourceRecords.title: Conformity and Obedience (by Jerry M. Burger, Santa Clara University)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (nobaproject.com is live; module page read directly 2026-08-22). Supports: the two primary reasons for conformity (concern about what others think — normative influence — and others as a source of information — informational influence); the Asch study description with 16 cards, 12 critical trials, and 76% conforming at least once; replication findings (conformity increases with confederates up to about five, teenagers conform more than adults, less conformity when responses are private; Bond, 2005; Bond & Smith, 1996); the culture finding (effect in virtually every culture studied, higher in collectivist countries such as Japan and China than individualistic ones such as the United States); descriptive norms (Cialdini, Reno, & Kallgren, 1990) and misperceived norms and drinking (Neighbors et al., 2007). Module is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; used reference-only, no module prose adapted.
